## 0. Setup

Load the data.

```{r}
# Load the built-in mtcars dataset
data(mtcars)

# Show the first 6 rows to see the variables
head(mtcars)
```

## 1. Functions for summary statistics

Mean function.

```{r}
# Define a function that takes a numeric vector x
my_mean <- function(x) {
  # Add up all values and divide by how many there are
  sum(x) / length(x)
}
```

Variance function.

```{r}
# Define a function that takes a numeric vector x
my_var <- function(x) {
  # Compute the mean of x
  m <- mean(x)
  # Sum the squared distances from the mean and divide by n - 1
  sum((x - m)^2) / (length(x) - 1)
}
```

Standard deviation function.

```{r}
# Define a function that takes a numeric vector x
my_sd <- function(x) {
  # The standard deviation is the square root of the variance
  sqrt(my_var(x))
}
```

Standard error function.

```{r}
# Define a function that takes a numeric vector x
my_se <- function(x) {
  # Standard error = standard deviation divided by the square root of n
  my_sd(x) / sqrt(length(x))
}
```

Range function.

```{r}
# Define a function that takes a numeric vector x
my_range <- function(x) {
  # Return the largest value minus the smallest value
  max(x) - min(x)
}
```

## 2. Apply the functions to a variable

Apply the mean.

```{r}
# Apply my_mean to the mpg variable
my_mean(mtcars$mpg)
```

Apply the variance.

```{r}
# Apply my_var to the mpg variable
my_var(mtcars$mpg)
```

Apply the standard deviation.

```{r}
# Apply my_sd to the mpg variable
my_sd(mtcars$mpg)
```

Apply the standard error.

```{r}
# Apply my_se to the mpg variable
my_se(mtcars$mpg)
```

Apply the range.

```{r}
# Apply my_range to the mpg variable
my_range(mtcars$mpg)
```

Show that they work.

```{r}
# Compare my functions with R's built-in functions (each pair should match)
c(my_mean(mtcars$mpg), mean(mtcars$mpg))
c(my_var(mtcars$mpg),  var(mtcars$mpg))
c(my_sd(mtcars$mpg),   sd(mtcars$mpg))
```

**Result:** each pair prints two identical numbers, which proves the functions work.

Check them with `all.equal()`.

```{r}
# TRUE means the two results are the same (up to tiny rounding)
all.equal(my_mean(mtcars$mpg), mean(mtcars$mpg))
all.equal(my_sd(mtcars$mpg), sd(mtcars$mpg))
```

## 3. One function that returns all summary statistics

Define it.

```{r}
# Define a function that returns several statistics at once
summary_stats <- function(x) {
  # Put the results in a named vector so each value has a label
  c(n      = length(x),
    mean   = my_mean(x),
    sd     = my_sd(x),
    se     = my_se(x),
    min    = min(x),
    max    = max(x),
    range  = my_range(x))
}
```

Apply it to a variable.

```{r}
# Apply summary_stats to the mpg variable
summary_stats(mtcars$mpg)
```

**Result:** one named vector with n = 32 and the mean, sd, se, min, max, and range of mpg.

## 4. Function for the two-sample t-test (Welch)

Define it.

```{r}
# Define a function that takes two numeric vectors x and y
two_sample_t <- function(x, y) {
  # Sample sizes of each group
  n1 <- length(x)
  n2 <- length(y)
  # Means of each group
  m1 <- mean(x)
  m2 <- mean(y)
  # Variances of each group
  v1 <- var(x)
  v2 <- var(y)
  # Standard error of the difference between the means
  se <- sqrt(v1 / n1 + v2 / n2)
  # t statistic = difference in means divided by its standard error
  t_stat <- (m1 - m2) / se
  # Welch-Satterthwaite degrees of freedom
  df <- (v1 / n1 + v2 / n2)^2 /
        ((v1 / n1)^2 / (n1 - 1) + (v2 / n2)^2 / (n2 - 1))
  # Two-sided p-value from the t distribution
  p_value <- 2 * pt(-abs(t_stat), df)
  # 95% confidence interval for the difference in means
  ci <- (m1 - m2) + c(-1, 1) * qt(0.975, df) * se
  # Return everything in a list
  list(mean_x = m1, mean_y = m2, t = t_stat, df = df,
       p_value = p_value, conf_low = ci[1], conf_high = ci[2])
}
```

Split the data into two groups.

```{r}
# mpg of automatic cars (am = 0)
auto <- mtcars$mpg[mtcars$am == 0]

# mpg of manual cars (am = 1)
manual <- mtcars$mpg[mtcars$am == 1]
```

Apply the function.

```{r}
# Apply my t-test function to the two groups
two_sample_t(auto, manual)
```

Show that it works.

```{r}
# Run R's built-in Welch t-test on the same groups
t.test(auto, manual)
```

**Result:** the t statistic, degrees of freedom, p-value, and confidence interval from `two_sample_t()` match the built-in `t.test()` output. A p-value below 0.05 means the mean mpg differs between automatic and manual cars.

## 5. lapply()

`lapply(x, f, ...)` takes a list `x` and a function `f`, applies `f` to each element, and returns a new list.

Make a list of variables.

```{r}
# Put three variables into a named list
vars_list <- list(mpg = mtcars$mpg, hp = mtcars$hp, wt = mtcars$wt)
```

Apply a built-in function with lapply.

```{r}
# Apply mean to every element of the list (returns a list)
lapply(vars_list, mean)
```

Apply my own function with lapply.

```{r}
# Apply my summary_stats function to every element of the list
lapply(vars_list, summary_stats)
```

**Result:** a list with three elements (mpg, hp, wt), each holding its own summary statistics.

Apply the t-test function to several variables.

```{r}
# Names of the variables we want to compare between transmission types
test_vars <- c("mpg", "hp", "wt", "disp")

# For each variable, run my t-test on automatic (am = 0) vs manual (am = 1)
t_results <- lapply(test_vars, function(v) {
  two_sample_t(mtcars[mtcars$am == 0, v], mtcars[mtcars$am == 1, v])
})

# Name each result with its variable
names(t_results) <- test_vars
```

View the results.

```{r}
# Show the full t-test result for every variable
t_results
```

Extract only the p-values.

```{r}
# Pull out the p-value from each result (lapply returns a list)
lapply(t_results, function(r) r$p_value)
```

**Result:** a list of four p-values, one for each variable. Those below 0.05 show a significant difference between automatic and manual cars.
